lesson.title: Why Every Differentiable Function Is Continuous
lesson.summary: If a function has a derivative at a point, it must also be continuous there, because a well-defined finite slope forces the function's value to change smoothly as the input approaches that point.
lesson.body:
Differentiability is a strictly stronger condition than continuity: every function that is differentiable at a point is automatically continuous there, though as later sections show, the reverse implication fails. This one-directional relationship is one of the most useful facts in calculus, because it means that once you have shown a function is differentiable somewhere, continuity there comes for free, and it also means that if you can show a function is discontinuous somewhere, you already know without further work that it cannot be differentiable there either.

The proof is a clean piece of limit algebra. Suppose f is differentiable at a, meaning f'(a) = lim as x approaches a of [f(x) - f(a)] / (x - a) exists as a finite number. To show continuity, it suffices to show that lim as x approaches a of [f(x) - f(a)] equals 0, since that is equivalent to lim f(x) equaling f(a). Write f(x) - f(a) as the product of two pieces: [f(x) - f(a)] / (x - a), multiplied by (x - a). As x approaches a, the first factor approaches f'(a) by the definition of the derivative, and the second factor, x - a, approaches 0. Since both limits exist, the limit of the product is the product of the limits, so lim [f(x) - f(a)] = f'(a) times 0 = 0. This shows f(x) approaches f(a) as x approaches a, which is precisely the statement that f is continuous at a.

A concrete illustration makes the mechanism tangible. Take f(x) = x^2 at a = 3. The derivative is f'(x) = 2x, so f'(3) = 6, a finite number, meaning f is differentiable at 3. According to the theorem, f must therefore be continuous at 3 as well, and indeed it is: as x approaches 3, x^2 approaches 9, which is exactly f(3). Tracing through the proof with actual numbers, [f(x) - f(3)] / (x - 3) = (x^2 - 9) / (x - 3) = x + 3 for x not equal to 3, which approaches 6 as x approaches 3, confirming f'(3) = 6, while the factor (x - 3) approaches 0, so their product, f(x) - f(3), correctly approaches 0.

The importance of this result is mostly as a diagnostic shortcut. If a function has a jump, a hole, or a vertical asymptote at some point, meaning it fails to be continuous there, there is no need to even attempt computing a derivative at that point, since discontinuity already rules out differentiability entirely. This is why the very first step in checking whether a piecewise function is differentiable at a boundary point is always to check continuity first: it is a necessary condition, and confirming it before computing one-sided derivatives saves wasted effort whenever it fails.

It is worth stating the logical direction precisely, since it is easy to misremember: differentiable implies continuous, not the other way around. The next section explores exactly this asymmetry, showing that continuity alone guarantees nothing about the existence of a derivative.
